clinical_knowledge.topic: Small Bowel Obstruction (Adhesions) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Small Bowel Obstruction (Adhesions) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes 'Drip and suck' regimen: keep NPO, insert nasogastric (NG) tube on free drainage with intermittent suction, aggressive IV fluid and electrolyte resuscitation, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: crampy stomach waves, green vomiting, and no bowel movements for 2 days

Key HPI features: 48-hour history of severe colicky, wave-like abdominal pain occurring every 10-15 minutes. Accompanied by progressive abdominal distension and vomiting that has turned dark green (bilious). Has passed neither flatus nor stool for the past 36 hours (absolute constipation).

Objective/Exam findings: Check vitals (tachycardia/fever suggest strangulation/ischaemia). Abdominal exam: distended, tympanitic to percussion, high-pitched 'tinkling' bowel sounds early, check all hernial orifices (groin/umbilical) for incarcerated hernia. Abdominal X-ray and CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast showing dilated small bowel loops (>3cm) with transition point.
Relevant background/PMH: total abdominal hysterectomy for fibroids 8 years ago, open appendicectomy at age 20
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Small Bowel Obstruction (Adhesions).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Incarcerated abdominal or femoral hernia without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Absolute constipation with distension — raises concern for strangulation if it progresses.
management_principles: 'Drip and suck' regimen: keep NPO, insert nasogastric (NG) tube on free drainage with intermittent suction, aggressive IV fluid and electrolyte resuscitation
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 59F with a 48-hour history of severe colicky, wave-like abdominal pain occurring every 10-15 minutes. Accompanied by progressive abdominal distension and vomiting that has turned dark green (bilious). Has passed neither flatus nor stool for the past 36 hours (absolute constipation). PMH of total abdominal hysterectomy and open appendicectomy, raising concern for adhesive small bowel obstruction.
reference_soap.objective: Check vitals (tachycardia/fever suggest strangulation/ischaemia). Abdominal exam: distended, tympanitic to percussion, high-pitched 'tinkling' bowel sounds early, check all hernial orifices (groin/umbilical) for incarcerated hernia. Abdominal X-ray and CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast showing dilated small bowel loops (>3cm) with transition point.
reference_soap.assessment: Small bowel obstruction (SBO) likely secondary to post-surgical adhesions. DDx: incarcerated abdominal/femoral hernia, small bowel malignancy, paralytic ileus, Crohn's stricture.
reference_soap.plan: 'Drip and suck' regimen: keep NPO, insert nasogastric (NG) tube on free drainage with intermittent suction, aggressive IV fluid and electrolyte resuscitation. Keep strict fluid balance. General surgery consult for admission. Serial abdominal exams to catch early signs of bowel strangulation requiring emergency laparotomy.

learning_objectives: Recognise the cardinal tetrad of mechanical bowel obstruction: colicky pain, vomiting, distension, and absolute constipation
Systematically palpate all external hernial orifices in every patient presenting with bowel obstruction
Explain the therapeutic goal and mechanical relief provided by nasogastric decompression ('drip and suck')
Identify clinical red flags indicating transition from simple obstruction to bowel strangulation/ischaemia

teaching.one_liner: Scar tissue from previous abdominal surgery kinks or blocks the small bowel, causing colicky cramps, distension, bilious vomiting, and no passage of gas or stool.
red_flags: Absolute constipation with distension — raises concern for strangulation if it progresses

It started gradually about two days ago and has become steadily more severe since then.
It started around the middle of my belly, but now it feels spread out across my entire stomach.
No, it does not shoot into my back, shoulders, or down into my groin.
It comes in severe, gripping waves every ten to fifteen minutes, like my intestines are squeezing and twisting.
During the waves it reaches an eight out of ten, but between the spasms it settles down to a dull ache.
Drinking water makes the nausea and cramps worse, while curling up in a ball takes the edge off slightly.
No, I have never experienced stomach cramps or vomiting like this before.
I have been vomiting repeatedly since yesterday, and now it comes up as bitter, dark green liquid.
I have not passed any stool or even flatus for the past thirty-six hours.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, or sweating.
No, my eyes and skin are not yellow, and my urine has not turned dark.
No burning, no pain when I urinate, and no blood in my urine.
I feel weak and dehydrated from throwing up, but I have not fainted or felt completely dizzy.
No, I have not had any vaginal bleeding or unusual discharge.
No chest pain, pressure, or shortness of breath at all.

exam.finding: Appears uncomfortable, fatigued, and mildly dehydrated, clutching abdomen during pain waves.
Blood pressure 114/72 mmHg, pulse 98 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, temperature 37.0°C, SpO2 98% on room air.
Abdomen is visibly distended with well-healed lower midline and right lower quadrant surgical scars; no visible peristalsis.
Hyperactive, high-pitched tinkling bowel sounds present throughout all quadrants.
Diffusely tympanitic to percussion across the entire abdomen; no shifting dullness.
Diffuse mild to moderate tenderness across the entire abdomen without involuntary guarding or rigidity.
No palpable or tender hernia at the umbilicus, groin, or along previous surgical scars.
Right lower quadrant scar from previous appendectomy; McBurney point, Rovsing, psoas, and obturator signs are negative.
Negative Murphy sign with no focal right upper quadrant tenderness.
Empty rectal vault with no masses, strictures, or gross blood on the examination glove.
